sentences.text: A solar water heater uses energy from the sun to warm the water a household needs.
The most common design for homes has two main parts: a flat collector fixed to the roof and a storage tank placed above or near it.
Because it has no engine, the system makes almost no noise.
The collector is a shallow box with a sheet of glass on top.
Under the glass lies a dark metal plate, which absorbs sunlight and turns it into heat.
Narrow copper pipes run across the plate and carry water through the collector.
A layer of insulation behind the plate stops the heat from escaping through the back of the box.
The system needs no pump when the tank sits higher than the collector.
Cold water first enters the bottom of the collector from a pipe connected to the tank.
As the water in the pipes warms, it becomes lighter and rises to the top of the collector.
From there it flows into the upper part of the tank, while cooler water from the bottom of the tank moves down to replace it.
This slow circulation continues for as long as the sun shines on the glass.
When someone opens a hot tap, the hottest water is drawn from the top of the tank.
Solar heaters work best in sunny regions, but they are also used in cooler countries.
In winter, a small electric heater inside the tank can raise the temperature on cloudy days.
Owners are advised to clean the glass twice a year, since dust can reduce the amount of light that reaches the plate.
With this simple care, a well-built system can last for more than twenty years.

sentences.text: For most of history, books were rare and expensive objects.
The collections that did exist belonged to temples, universities and wealthy families, and few ordinary people could use them.
This began to change in the nineteenth century, when several towns opened libraries paid for by local taxes.
Supporters argued that free access to books would help working people educate themselves.
Critics, however, worried about the cost to taxpayers.
Early public libraries looked very different from today's.
Readers could not take books from the shelves themselves; instead, they asked a librarian, who fetched each volume from a closed store.
Open shelves, where visitors choose freely, became common only in the early twentieth century.
Children were often not allowed inside the first public libraries.
The first separate children's rooms appeared around 1900, with smaller furniture and books written for young readers.
Within a few decades, story hours and reading clubs had made children some of the most regular visitors.
Today, many libraries lend far more than books.
Visitors can borrow laptops, use study rooms and join language classes.
Some libraries even lend tools or musical instruments, and most offer free internet access.
Even so, librarians report that quiet reading space is still among the services people value most.

For a long time, sleep was seen simply as a period of rest for the body.
Over the last fifty years, however, researchers have shown that the brain remains very active while we sleep.
In my view, this discovery is one of the most important in modern psychology.
Much of this activity seems to support memory.
In one well-known study, Dr Lena Hartmann asked students to learn a list of word pairs in the evening.
Students who then slept recalled more pairs the next morning than students who stayed awake for the same number of hours.
Hartmann concluded that sleep protects new memories from being disturbed.
Other researchers have looked at what happens during different stages of sleep.
Professor Ade Okafor found that deep sleep early in the night is linked to remembering facts, such as names and dates.
Later stages, which come mostly in the hours before waking, appear to help with skills, such as playing an instrument.
Cutting sleep short may therefore cost a learner more than they expect.
A third line of research concerns short daytime naps.
Dr Mei Tanaka reported that a nap of about twenty minutes improved attention in the afternoon.
Longer naps, she warned, can leave people feeling heavy and slow for a while after waking.
None of this means that students should sleep instead of studying.
Yet I believe schools that start very early in the morning are working against the way young people learn.
Whether later start times would raise exam results is a question that still needs careful study.
